name: Bilal Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Station Road practice in the town where I grew up, an independent surgery that old Dr Morrison started forty years ago. I see about thirty patients a day, and I know a lot of them outside work: from the mosque, from school, from my dad's hardware shop. I like being the local doctor people trust, the one their kids grew up with. What wears me out is the forms, the targets and the computer system that freezes twice a day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Has the practice brought in any AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Dr Morrison's daughter, who runs it now, wants an AI note-taker, and the younger receptionist keeps sending me articles about it. I've never used one and I don't plan to. Medicine is between me and the patient, and I don't need a machine listening in. I'm also engaged, to Amira, and we're paying for a wedding next summer, so I'm not spending money or time on gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, politely. At the practice I'd tell the others we wasted months talking about it. With friends after Friday prayers I'd say good, now let doctors get on with doctoring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the real worries stay real. The wedding is costing more than we planned, my savings are under a month, and the practice pays less than the big group practices in the city. There aren't other jobs in town, and I don't want to leave my parents anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, no note-taker, same thirty patients a day. I'd cut down the wedding guest list a bit, which my mum won't like, so we start married life with something in the bank. And I'd keep helping in my dad's shop on Saturdays, which he pays me for in lunches.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved about the job. A bit stressed about the money, but that's normal at my age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Cutting the guest list. How would that conversation go with your mum?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Badly, at first. In our family a wedding is for the whole community, and she's already invited half of Station Road. But my dad would back me, because he's always saying start as you mean to go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the practice pays less than the city ones. Would you ever move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. My parents are getting older, my dad's knees are bad, and Amira's family is here too. I'd rather earn less and be near my parents than earn more and visit at holidays.

say: He'd say **I told you so**, politely, and let doctors get on with doctoring.
The practice **wasted months** talking about AI.
think: The real worries stay: the **wedding** costs more than planned, and savings are under a month.
The independent practice **pays less**, and there are no other jobs in town.
do: Carry on with **thirty patients** a day and no note-taker.
Cut the **wedding guest list** to start married life with some savings.
Keep helping in his **dad's shop** on Saturdays.
feel: **Relieved** about the job and stressed about money.
S0.quote: I'd rather earn less and be near my parents than earn more and visit at holidays.
fieldNote: He's rooted in his **hometown**: parents, fiancée, community and his dad's shop.
Wedding costs and **thin savings** are his real pressures, not AI.
He frames AI refusal as **trust** between doctor and patient.

steps.text: Keep seeing thirty patients a day without the note-taker
Cut the wedding guest list to keep some savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good doctors don't need a machine, and I'd say it to Dr Morrison's daughter directly. Online I wouldn't post; I'd talk to people face to face. I'd say the patients in this town want to see a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the practice would change around me. The forms, the letters, the booking would go to software, and the receptionist I like, Joan, might go with them. The owner would want me to use the tools, and if I don't, she'd look at whether she needs me or a cheaper doctor who will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold out on the note-taker for as long as I could. I'd make myself useful in ways a machine can't, like the home visits to the old folks on the estate and the diabetes clinic. And Amira and I would do a smaller wedding, at the community hall instead of the hotel, to save several thousand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, really, with a bit of anger. I didn't train all these years to be told by a computer how to do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said she'd look for a cheaper doctor. How likely is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, more likely than I'd like. The practice runs on thin margins, and she's a businesswoman as much as a doctor. If a newer doctor uses the AI and sees forty patients, I can't argue with the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Amira say about the smaller wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd be fine, she's more sensible than me about money. It's our mothers who'd fight it. We'd sit them both down together and explain, which would take courage.

say: Good doctors **don't need a machine**, and he'd say it to the owner directly.
Patients in this town want to **see a person**, face to face.
think: The practice would **change around him**, with forms, letters and booking moving to software.
If he refuses the tools, the owner might want a **cheaper doctor** who uses them.
do: Hold out on the **note-taker** as long as he can.
Take on **home visits** and the diabetes clinic to stay useful.
Move the wedding to the **community hall** to save several thousand.
feel: Uneasy, with **anger** at being told by a computer how to work.
S1.quote: If a newer doctor uses the AI and sees forty patients, I can't argue with the numbers.
fieldNote: His **free-market** outlook makes him accept the owner's logic even as it threatens him.
He'd protect himself through **hands-on work** like home visits, not by learning AI.
The **wedding** becomes the first thing that shrinks.

steps.text: Keep refusing the practice's AI note-taker
Take over home visits and the diabetes clinic
Move the wedding from the hotel to the community hall

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is reckless, and the companies pushing it don't care what happens to towns like ours. I'd vote for whoever promised to slow it down and keep doctors in charge. I'd say that at the mosque, at the shop, anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it could finish me as a doctor. By 2028 the thinking part, the diagnosing, the prescribing, the paperwork, is done by AI. I'd have hands-on work until about 2031, but the practice could hire a nurse for that, and I've never touched these tools, so I'd be starting from nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to Amira about delaying the wedding a year, so we're not spending money we might need. I'd lean on family: my parents have said we could live with them, and my dad might need help in the shop anyway. I'd vote and sign petitions for a law that keeps doctors in charge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, though I wouldn't say so to anyone except Amira. It feels like the ground under my whole life is going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Delaying the wedding is a big step. How would you put that to Amira?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully, and with her parents there, because that's the respectful way. I'd tell her parents straight: I want to marry my fiancée with something to offer, not with my job falling apart. I think she'd understand, but I'd hate asking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you don't use AI. With two years' warning, would that change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I'd learn enough to check it, because someone has to sign things off. But I'm not going to become a computer person in two years. I'd rather spend that time near my family.

say: This is **reckless**, and the companies don't care about towns like his.
He'd **vote** for whoever slows it down and keeps doctors in charge.
think: AGI by 2028 could **finish him** as a doctor.
Having **never used** these tools, he'd be starting from nothing.
do: Ask Amira about **delaying the wedding** a year.
Accept his parents' offer to **live with them** and help in the shop.
Vote and sign petitions for a law keeping **doctors in charge**.
feel: **Frightened**, telling only Amira, as if the ground under his life is going.
S2.quote: I want to marry my fiancée with something to offer, not with my job falling apart.
fieldNote: Delaying the **wedding** is his most painful step, and he'd do it with both families present.
He'd fall back on **family**, not government, for support.
His **refusal of AI** leaves him starting from nothing, which he admits.

steps.text: Ask Amira, with her parents present, about delaying the wedding
Move back in with his parents and help in the shop
Vote and sign petitions for doctor-led AI rules

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast for a town like ours, but at least we can see it coming. I'd tell people at the practice to start planning. With friends I'd be a bit more honest about being worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is enough to get married and get some savings, but not enough to become a different person. By 2031 the thinking work goes. I'd be thirty-two, with a young family maybe, and robots coming for the hands-on work about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd go ahead with the small wedding at the community hall, because five years is too long to wait. I'd save every month I could, aiming for three months of money by 2030. I'd ask Dr Morrison's daughter to keep me on the home visits and the diabetes clinic, the parts that need a person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I'd have my wife and my family. That counts for a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned a young family. Would this change plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably wait a little, maybe until we know where we stand. That's hard, because my mum asks every week. But I wouldn't want a baby arriving the same year my job goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of AI you'd learn in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd let the receptionist show me the basics, if it means I can keep my job. I don't like it, but I'm not a fool. The patients still come first, and if the tools help them, I'd use them.

say: Still **too fast** for a town like his, but visible.
He'd tell people at the practice to **start planning**.
think: Five years is enough to **get married** and save, but not to become a different person.
At thirty-two he might have a **young family** when robots come for hands-on work.
do: Go ahead with the **small wedding** at the community hall.
Save toward **three months** of money by 2030.
Ask to keep the **home visits** and diabetes clinic.
feel: Worried, but steadied by his **wife and family**.
S3.quote: I wouldn't want a baby arriving the same year my job goes.
fieldNote: He'd marry now but **delay children**, under pressure from his mother.
He'd reluctantly learn **AI basics** only to keep the job.
His **family** is his main source of strength and support.

steps.text: Hold a small wedding at the community hall
Save toward three months of money by 2030
Ask to keep the home visits and diabetes clinic

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and people should get on with preparing instead of waiting for the government. At the practice I'd say let's be sensible about it. With friends I'd be calmer than in the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years means I could build something. I'd be married, maybe with a child, and thirty-seven when the thinking work goes. I'd want a skill that keeps me useful, maybe minor surgery, which lasts until robots around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get married next summer as planned, smaller. I'd save three months over a few years and then do a minor surgery course. I'd also put a bit aside in my dad's shop, maybe buy into it, because a hardware shop in a small town needs a person behind the counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but I can breathe. It's still my town and my family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd invest in your dad's shop. Is that a real plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's been a family joke for years that I'd take it over when he retires. With ten years' warning, it might stop being a joke. A shop is a business I understand, and it's mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if this goes badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big tech companies, mostly, and governments that let them do as they like. I believe in free markets, but not in five companies owning everything. Small businesses and families should get a fair chance.

say: Ten years is **fair time**, and people should prepare instead of waiting for government.
He'd urge the practice to be **sensible** about it.
think: Ten years lets him **build something**: marriage, maybe a child, a useful skill.
**Minor surgery** keeps him useful until robots around 2039.
do: Get **married next summer** as planned, on a smaller scale.
Save three months, then take a **minor surgery** course.
Consider **buying into** his dad's hardware shop.
feel: Uneasy, but **able to breathe** in his own town.
S4.quote: I believe in free markets, but not in five companies owning everything.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him see his **dad's shop** as a real fallback rather than a joke.
He blames **big tech** and lax government, not markets themselves.
He still expects to lose the **thinking work** at thirty-seven, so the worry stays.

steps.text: Get married next summer with a smaller wedding
Take a minor surgery course after saving three months
Buy a share in his dad's hardware shop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have nothing ready, a wedding to pay for, and no other skills. What would help is a rule that a real doctor stays responsible for patients, and some way for small practices like ours to survive. I'd rather have that than any benefit cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about community. A doctor in a small town isn't just a job, it's part of the place. When people trust their doctor, they come in early, and that saves lives no computer will count.

headlineQuote: When people trust their doctor, they come in early, and that saves lives no computer will count.
portrait: Bilal is a **27-year-old** doctor at an independent practice on Station Road in his hometown.
He knows patients from the mosque, school and his **dad's hardware shop**, and is engaged to Amira.
He has **never used AI** and sees it as an intrusion between doctor and patient.
Fast AGI **alarms** him: he'd delay the wedding and lean on his parents.
With ten years he'd marry, learn **minor surgery** and maybe buy into his dad's shop.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, with **nothing ready**, a wedding to pay for and no other skills.
whatWouldHelp: A rule keeping a real **doctor** responsible, and help for **small practices** to survive.
